paragraphs: Boosting improves classification by combining base classifiers. This paper addresses two concerns about AdaBoost and existing boosting approaches: AdaBoost can overfit, particularly when data contain noise, and fixed combination weights do not account for the particular input being classified. The authors ask whether changing how classifier contributions are weighted can help address both concerns.

Their algorithm, WeightBoost, introduces a regularization factor that depends on the input into the combination weight. This makes the weighting responsive to the input pattern while adding regularization intended to address overfitting. The authors also derive a learning procedure, analogous to AdaBoost’s, with a guarantee of minimizing training errors. That guarantee concerns performance on training data; the paper separately evaluates classification accuracy and noise robustness through experiments.

Across eight UCI datasets and one text categorization dataset, WeightBoost achieves considerably higher classification accuracy than AdaBoost in almost all of the reported comparisons. Experiments that artificially control the amount of noise also indicate greater robustness than AdaBoost. Together, these findings support input-dependent regularization as a promising way to improve boosting’s accuracy and handling of noise, with the reported advantage being empirical and nearly, rather than entirely, consistent across the evaluated datasets.
icml-2003-a-new-boosting-algorithm-using.tldr: WeightBoost adds input-dependent regularization to classifier combination weights, achieving better accuracy than AdaBoost in almost all reported dataset comparisons and showing greater noise robustness experimentally.
